title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
summary:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s…

blocks.text: China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.
China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.
The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.
Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged.

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

blocks.caption: Chen Jining waves the Paralympic flag during the Closing Ceremony for the 2018 Winter Paralympics in South Korea, in his role as mayor of Beijing.  Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

blocks.text: He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.
Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University, called it a reminder of “how little we really understand about what’s going on in Chinese elite politics”.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign, which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged, including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.
“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ’self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.

Chen, who last appeared in public last week, was a good candidate to ​watch for elevation to the ‌politburo standing committee in the ​party’s top reshuffle next year, Mittelstaedt said. “This ​sends a signal that nobody is safe.”
The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.
Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.
